title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics
book_title: Chapter 3: How It Is Sold & Delivered — OEM Logistics, Working Capital & Unit Economics
question: How does GNA Axles move forged steel from Punjab to North American and Indian assembly lines, why do debtor days sit at 151 days, and how does ₹100 of FY26 revenue cascade down to Free Cash Flow?

epigraph.quote: Revenue is vanity, operating margin is sanity, but working-capital days are reality.
epigraph.author: Industrial Cash-Flow Maxim

web_blocks.title: Direct OEM Qualification & Global Delivery Mechanics

web_blocks.html: Consumer brands sell through distributors or retail dealers. By contrast, GNA Axles runs a 100% direct B2B OEM and Tier-1 supply model [5][11]. No middlemen take a 10%–15% wholesale cut. To win a new platform, GNA's metallurgists and tooling engineers co-develop prototypes with an OEM's drivetrain team. They submit PPAP (Production Part Approval Process) samples and complete 12 to 24 months of fatigue-rig and field tests [5][7]. Once approved, GNA receives rolling quarterly schedules and monthly call-offs.

Domestically (~53% of sales), GNA trucks finished shafts straight from Mehtiana and Gulabgarh Jattan to plants across Punjab, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, and Haryana [7][10]. For exports (~47% of sales), workers rust-proof and palletize parts, then send them by rail or truck to Mundra and Nhava Sheva ports [5][10]. Ocean freight carries them to North America, South America, Europe, and Asia. Destination warehouses then handle just-in-time delivery to Dana, Cummins-Meritor, and John Deere plants [11]. GNA buys specialty alloy steel bars from qualified Indian and global mills under quarterly or semi-annual pass-through clauses. When steel prices jump, revenue rises and percentage margins dip slightly on paper, while absolute rupee profit per shaft stays protected.

web_blocks.title: The 151-Day Receivable Puzzle & Export Credit Financing

web_blocks.html: Now let us look past the clean P&L to check balance sheet friction. In FY26, GNA's Debtor Days stood at 151 days. That was up from 119–130 days pre-COVID and flat against 151 days in FY25 [1]. Combined with 117 Inventory Days and 129 Days Payable, GNA's net Cash Conversion Cycle reached 139 days (Working Capital Days: 133 days) [1]. Why does GNA wait five months to collect cash?

Two structural forces explain the 151-day DSO. First, ocean transit to the Americas and Europe plus customs and warehousing take 45–60 days. Only then does the clock start on standard 60–90 day OEM credit terms. Second, global Tier-1s like Dana and Meritor hold strong bargaining power over mid-cap suppliers. To bridge this five-month gap, GNA uses low-cost Packing Credit in Foreign Currency (PCFC) and bill-discounting export credit. That kept FY26 finance costs at just ₹13 Cr on ₹1,478 Cr of sales [1][2]. Still, 151 debtor days acts as a structural tax on ROCE. Every ₹100 Cr of new export sales locks up roughly ₹36–40 Cr in net working capital.

To remove guesswork, let us trace every ₹100 of GNA's audited FY26 revenue (₹1,478.4 Cr). We will follow it through factory costs, overhead, taxes, working capital, and capex to see what became Free Cash Flow [1][2]:

web_blocks.takeaway: In FY26, GNA converted ₹100 of revenue into ₹16.13 of EBITDA and ₹7.91 of PAT; aided by payable timing, CFO hit ₹14.48 per ₹100, leaving ₹3.79 of FCF after heavy ₹10.69 reinvestment in capex [1][2].

web_blocks.mechanism: Accuride supplied steel/aluminum wheels and wheel-end components directly to North American Class 8 truck and trailer OEMs—facing the exact same freight-cycle volatility, OEM working-capital terms, and heavy fixed-asset forging/stamping intensity as GNA Axles.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: When the 2023–2024 US freight recession hit Class 8 builds, Accuride's $500M–$1B liability stack and >$400M funded debt overwhelmed operating cash flows, forcing a voluntary Chapter 11 bankruptcy filing on October 9, 2024; lenders equitized >85% of debt before emergence in March 2025 [15].
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: Cyclical Class 8 component suppliers die from leverage, not from bad engineering. GNA's conservative balance sheet (₹203 Cr total borrowings vs ₹1,074 Cr equity) is the single reason it sailed through the same 2024–2025 US freight slump without distress [1].

book_paragraphs: Let us walk through how a rupee of GNA revenue is earned, collected, and turned into cash—because in heavy forging, the P&L tells only half the story. GNA does not sell through retail dealers or aftermarket wholesalers. Every rupee comes from direct B2B contracts with OEMs and Tier-1 drivetrain integrators [5][11]. Winning a part number takes 12 to 24 months of metallurgical testing and PPAP sign-offs, after which GNA ships directly from Punjab to tractor plants in India or via Mundra port to Dana, Cummins-Meritor, and John Deere facilities in North America and Europe [7][11].

On the cost side, GNA's unit economics are disciplined. Alloy steel bars account for roughly 61% of revenue (₹904.4 Cr net of inventory changes on ₹1,478.4 Cr sales in FY26), and most OEM contracts carry raw-material pass-through clauses that insulate absolute rupee spreads when steel prices swing [1][2]. Because Mehtiana and Gulabgarh Jattan rely heavily on automated upsetters, robotic material handling, and CNC cells, employee costs consume just 5.9% of sales (₹87.2 Cr) [2][7]. After ₹248.4 Cr in power, fuel, tooling, and freight overhead, GNA kept ₹238.4 Cr—or ₹16.13 out of every ₹100 of sales—as Operating EBITDA in FY26 [1][2].

Now look at the friction point: collections. GNA's Debtor Days hit 151 days in both FY25 and FY26 [1]. That means five full months of sales sit unpaid on the balance sheet at any given moment. Why? Partly because ocean freight and destination warehousing eat up 45–60 days before OEM credit clocks even start, and partly because global giants like Dana and Meritor dictate payment terms. GNA finances that gap cheaply using foreign-currency export credit (keeping FY26 interest at just ₹13 Cr), and in FY26 an expansion in Days Payable (from 76 to 129 days) helped lift Cash Flow from Operations to ₹214 Cr [1].

Still, you and I should not confuse a one-year payable timing boost with structural capital lightness. Over the long run, 151 debtor days means GNA must reinvest heavily in working capital and ₹100–125 Cr of annual capex just to grow [1][5]. That is also why GNA's low debt (₹203 Cr borrowings) is non-negotiable: as Accuride Corporation's October 2024 Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the US Class 8 wheel-end market proved, mixing North American truck cyclicality with heavy debt is fatal [15].

book_subsections.title: Tracing ₹100 of FY26 Revenue to Free Cash Flow
paragraphs: Let us walk through the exact audited FY26 waterfall so there is zero guesswork [1][2]. Out of every ₹100 of GNA's ₹1,478.4 Cr revenue, ₹61.17 went to direct alloy-steel materials (adjusted for inventory changes), ₹5.90 covered lean automated payroll, and ₹16.80 paid for power, forging fuel, freight, and overhead [1][2]. That left ₹16.13 in Operating EBITDA [1]. Subtracting ₹4.73 for depreciation, ₹0.88 for low-cost export-credit interest, adding ₹0.20 of other income, and paying ₹2.80 in corporate taxes left ₹7.91 in reported Net Profit [1][2].

Below the profit line, an expansion in supplier payables helped lift Cash Flow from Operations to ₹14.48 per ₹100 of revenue (₹214 Cr total) [1]. Because GNA reinvested ₹10.69 per ₹100 (₹158 Cr) into new forging and SUV/EV machining lines, Free Cash Flow landed at ₹3.79 per ₹100 (₹56 Cr) [1]. That is a respectable, self-funded cash engine—provided you remember that in years like FY25 when payables do not stretch, FCF can temporarily dip negative (-₹18 Cr) [1].

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: The Working-Capital Tax on Export Ambition
book_callouts.text: Every time you see an Indian auto-ancillary company boast about rising export share, check its Debtor Days immediately. Shipping steel parts across oceans to Detroit or Brazil looks glamorous on a slide deck, but it stretches the cash conversion cycle from 60 days to 139 days [1]. In FY26, GNA generated ₹214 Cr of CFO and ₹56 Cr of Free Cash Flow after ₹158 Cr of capex—a healthy result [1]. Yet in FY25, when payables did not stretch, CFO was ₹92 Cr and FCF was negative ₹18 Cr [1]. Always underwrite GNA's multi-year cumulative cash flow, never a single peak year.
